newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan voters humble once mighty Socialists.
newsitem.headline: Japan voters humble once mighty Socialists.

text.p: Japanese voters, ignoring the Social Democratic Party's campaign call to "keep the torch burning", reduced the once-fiery, 50-year-old leftist group to a shadow of its former self.

The Social Democrats, which began life as a protest force against the pro-business, pro-U.S. Liberal Democratic Party and ended up for a while as the LDP's coalition partner, saw their seats in parliament's Lower House cut in half.

"It was, as predicted, a very severe outcome for us," party head Takako Doi said early on Monday of a tally which reduced her party to 15 seats from its previous 30 in the 500-seat Lower House of parliament.
The party was expected to face a tough decision on whether to join in a coalition with the LDP, which needs the Social Democrats' 36 seats in the less influential Upper House.

Doi, a staunch leftist ideologue whose vigorous leadership of the party from 1986-91 prompted admirers to compare her to Margaret Thatcher, was renamed as chief last month in a last-ditch bid to revive the Social Democrats' fortunes.

Sunday's snub was only the latest in a string of electoral setbacks and defections in recent years which saw the party's strength in the powerful Lower House fall from 136 seats in 1990 to the 30 it had when polls began this month.

The Social Democrats' slide began in the 1990s as voters showed they didn't trust a party of perennial oppositionists who spent their lives howling at the LDP from the political wilderness and sought moderate alternatives to its uncompromising leftist defence and foreign policies.
Labour unions that traditionally backed the Social Democrats, hedging their bets at a time of economic uncertainty and unemployment fears, began shopping for new parties to protect their interests.
The party's decline quickened in 1994 when party leader Tomiichi Murayama became Japan's first Socialist prime minister in 40 years -- at the top of a coalition dominated by its arch-foe the LDP.

Shortly after taking office, Murayama scrapped his party's traditional left-wing Cold War-era policies, such as opposition to the security treaty under which U.S. troops are stationed in Japan and refusal to accept Japan's flag and national anthem.
The policy about-face undercut Murayama's standing in the party by deepening a long-standing rift between the party's left and right wings.

Part of the left wing splintered off last year to form the New Socialist Party, dedicated to pacifism and traditional leftist policies, while most of the right-wing last month bolted to join the newly formed Democratic Party.

A fatigued Murayama resigned as prime minister in January, after a tenure which saw a killer earthquake, a terrorist attack on Tokyo's subways, banking failures and unprecedented disputes over the presence of the U.S. military.
Many critics said the nation's woes had been exacerbated by the weak leadership of the left-right coalition.

Shortly after Murayama's resignation, the party changed its Japanese name from the Socialists to Social Democratic Party -- five years after it had changed its English name -- in what critics said was a piecemeal step symbolic of its inability to adopt to a changing post-Cold War political scene.
